title: The Summit of the Gods
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: In 1993 Kathmandu, Japanese photographer Makoto Fukamachi finds an old camera that may have belonged to George Mallory, who vanished on Everest in 1924, but it is taken by a reclusive climber he suspects is Joji Habu, a legendary solo alpinist who disappeared years before. Fukamachi digs into Habu's obsessive, self-destructive climbing life and his rivalry with Tsuneo Hase, and is drawn toward Everest himself. Adapted from Baku Yumemakura's novel (Wikipedia; Ponent Mon blurb; ANN House of 1000 Manga).
life_message: Giving everything to a pursuit beyond oneself can give life meaning, though obsession exacts a heavy price.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Rivalry with Hase and the drive to be first are matters of personal honor.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Habu climbs solo, outside expedition hierarchies.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is marginal; bonds are between climbers.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Climbing establishment and rankings versus loner outsiders.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular striving set against sacred Himalayan landscape.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival at altitude is constant, yet climbing is self-defining.

folkways.japan: Habu's single-minded devotion echoes the Japanese ideal of total commitment to one's path (michi), set mostly in Nepal.

delivery.evidence: Why-climb question recurs through Habu's life and Mallory's quote per ANN and Wikipedia.
delivery.note: Rival climbers and the toll on loved ones are shown seriously beside Habu's obsession.

winners_losers: The climbers' devotion earns admiration, but many die; sympathy goes to obsessive striving, with its toll on relationships shown.
